chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ismail, who said:

A man from our companions died and did not bequeath, so his matter was raised to the judge of Al-Kufa, and he appointed Abdul Hameed as the custodian of his wealth. The man had left behind young heirs, goods, and slave girls. Abdul Hameed sold the goods, but when he intended to sell the slave girls, his heart weakened regarding their sale, because the deceased had not appointed him as executor by will, and his custodianship was by the order of the judge, and because they are 'furuj' (chastity/sexual organs).

He said: So I mentioned that to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and said to him: A man from our companions dies and does not bequeath to anyone, and leaves behind slave girls, so the judge appoints a man from us to sell them, or said: A man from us is appointed to do that, but his heart weakens because they are 'furuj'. So what is your view regarding that? He said: If the custodian is like you and like Abdul Hameed, then there is no problem.

key_terms.فُرُوج: Chastity/Sexual organs (referring to integrity of slave girls)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on selling slave girls from an estate if the deceased did not appoint an executor?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the Shia juristic principle of *kafa'ah* (competence) in estate management, where the reliability of the custodian (*qayyim*) determines the validity of selling female slaves (*jawari*) from the deceased's assets. The Imam’s response highlights that the concern over their *furuj* (chastity or status) is mitigated when the seller is a trustworthy individual like the narrator or Abdul Hameed, reflecting the practical legal flexibility of the early Shia community in Kufa. It underscores the importance of personal integrity (*amanah*) in executing financial duties when no specific will is present.
